A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SFT/RFT forgetting study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocations and additions.

before.justification: V2 reports original jigsaw-training and prior-knowledge-retention experiments, including Tables 1–2 and learning-dynamics, perplexity, and restart analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains the original experiments and reports additional math reasoning, scientific QA, data-mixture, GRPO-recipe, and early-RFT results.

M1.justification: The core GRPO/SFT objectives, jigsaw rewards, periodic restarts, and rollout-supervision approach remain unchanged. Early-RFT trajectories followed by SFT were already described in v2 Section 6; v3 supplies more details and results without establishing a changed core procedure.

E1.justification: V3 adds text-only competition-style math training/evaluation using Open-Reasoner-Zero and scientific multiple-choice QA using Sci-MCQ4. GSM8K, MATH-500, and IFEval become additional retention benchmarks. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained jigsaw and multimodal evaluations.

E2.justification: Tables 7–8 add SFT-Mixture to comparisons with nonreasoning, GPT-4o-rollout, and GRPO-rollout SFT. Table 5 explicitly compares the early self-generated-data variant against RFT and rollout-based SFT. The principal comparator families remain unchanged; newly cited classical continual-learning methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Added protocols include 90/10 ORZ and Sci-MCQ4 splits, an 8,500-example science sample, Qwen2.5-Instruct experiments, four-rate math sweeps, and GRPO iteration settings of 1, 2, and 4. V3 also specifies the early-RFT budget. Algorithm 1 reports bicubic resizing, conflicting with the retained cropping description in Section 3.1; an actual preprocessing change is unresolved.

E4.justification: V3 adds equal-proportion reasoning/nonreasoning mixture ablations, GRPO iteration sensitivity, and math/science LBK and perplexity analyses, plus math Pareto and learning-rate analyses. The early-RFT study gains quantitative comparisons in Table 5. V2’s large-learning-rate jigsaw analysis is retained in Appendix E, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies independent training-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The 16-rollout perplexity boxplots already appear in v2 Figure 4; v3 extends existing graphical reporting conventions without disclosing a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results, including GRPO-rollout SFT ORZ accuracies of 37.8%/53.4% for 3B/7B, Sci-MCQ4 accuracy of 71.7%, and 84.0% jigsaw accuracy for the 3B early-RFT-derived SFT variant. These are newly reported experiments. Original Table 1 is unchanged. In v2 Table 2 versus v3 Table 4, the 7B base MME entry changes from 2334 to 2333; remaining score differences are rounding.

T1.justification: Theorems 5.1–5.2, the eNTK/LBK mathematics, and the derivations and proofs in Appendices C–D remain unchanged. V3 adds explanatory prose and explicitly states standard GRPO advantage normalization without revising the formal argument.

C1.justification: The abstract, three stated contributions, and central data-distribution explanation remain intact. V3’s conclusion adds the practical claim that even a short RFT phase can produce SFT data yielding RFT-comparable new-task performance while preserving knowledge better than GPT-4o-rollout SFT.

C2.justification: The early-RFT interpretation reverses: v2 describes a clear target-performance ceiling, while v3 Sections 5.8 and 6 argue that a short phase suffices for competitive performance. V3 also interprets mixture experiments as favoring distributional alignment over stylistic diversity and extends its mechanism interpretation to text tasks. Appendix B’s old jigsaw-only scope statement remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 adds preprocessing pseudocode, GPU-hour costs in Table 3, the TRL num_iterations setting, early-RFT budget and data-construction details, and GPT-4o prompts/examples for math and science. These materially expand implementation disclosure, although preprocessing descriptions conflict. The statement promising future code release is unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds Li and Hoiem and Chaudhry et al. to the existing continual-learning discussion, cites sources for the new tasks and models, and removes the InternVL3 citation and associated discussion. It clarifies that outperforming classical continual-learning algorithms is outside its aim; the main research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: V3 locally revises the introduction and learning-dynamics explanation, merges Discussion and Conclusion, and moves the large-learning-rate discussion to Appendix E. New sections and appendices organize the added studies, while the abstract, contribution list, and much of the original narrative remain unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 adds substantial visual reporting for math/science experiments, training costs, early-RFT results, mixture ablations, and GRPO sensitivity, together with Algorithm 1 and new prompt examples. Existing jigsaw figures are resized or relocated, and v2 Table 2 becomes appendix Table 4, producing substantial display and layout changes.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially reduces dependence on one unusual visual task through math/science evaluations and adds mixture and GRPO-recipe tests addressing alternative explanations. Table 5 supplies quantitative support for the previously performance-limited early-RFT approach, while cost and implementation disclosures improve practical assessment. Conflicting preprocessing descriptions, the outdated Appendix B scope statement, and overly uniform interpretations of some results reduce clarity, but the broader evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.
